<reason>Side A (CON) was sharper rhetorically and landed real hits on speed, leakage, and B's early "half-measures" escape hatch. But B recovered in Rebuttal 2 by supplying a concrete falsifiability test (take-up, queues, second-child intentions), which A kept denying existed, and by exposing A's fatal drift: A's only answer to the "dial" pressure was to make bonuses recurring and per-child, abandoning the motion's "one-off" policy. B's B4.4 point — that to match years of rent a bonus must become sustained support, which is housing and childcare by another name — was the decisive weighing, and B's fast-acting levers (rental support, fee caps in the next budget) blunted A's decade-scale timing attack without leaving the motion. A's closing doubled down on per-child recurring bonuses rather than answering that concession. B wins on motion fidelity and the unanswered completed-family-size argument, despite A's stronger delivery-mechanism exchanges.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side A's Q2 forced B to name fast-acting levers, and A's Rebuttal 2 spun this as a collapse ("their position has collapsed into mine"). But B's counter in B4.4 — that scaling the bonus until it matters means it "must stop being one-off and become sustained support, which is housing and childcare by another name" — turned A's own reframing into a concession that decided the motion.</best_rebuttal>
